finding.claim: Authorization bypass on DELETE /files/<fid>: the handler calls `require_allowed`, which is an import alias of the boolean `is_allowed` (views.py:4) rather than `ensure_allowed`. The returned False is discarded and nothing aborts, so the delete always proceeds. Any caller, including one with no grants or no user, can delete any file by id.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any or no X-Session-User-Verified header

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` aliases the predicate that returns a bool and never aborts
return value of require_allowed(...) is ignored, so the check has no effect

finding.guards_checked: Compared with the sibling rename_file (views.py:26), which uses ensure_allowed and aborts 403, so the control is enforced there but not here. There is no other auth middleware: before_request only sets g.user and does not reject. The only gate is the discarded check. A missing fid raises KeyError, which gives a 500 and not a bypass.

verdict.guard_found: before_request load_user (views.py:11-12) only sets g.user, no rejection; require_allowed is the bool is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:4-5) with its result discarded at views.py:18; no other auth middleware.
verdict.reason: views.py:18 calls the aliased boolean is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:5) as a bare statement, so nothing aborts and views.py:19 deletes any existing file for any anonymous caller, unlike rename_file's ensure_allowed at views.py:26.

finding.claim: Identity is taken directly from a client-supplied request header, `X-Session-User-Verified`, with no signature, session or token check. If the app is reachable without a front proxy that strips and sets this header, an attacker can impersonate any user named in a resource's grants and pass ensure_allowed (e.g. on rename). This depends on deployment, which cannot be confirmed from the code.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26, which authorizes by that identity and then allows the rename at views.py:27

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get(...) is the only authentication step
g.user is used as the principal for the authorization check
grants are looked up by that unauthenticated string

finding.guards_checked: No signature or session validation exists in the code I read. No proxy or deployment config is present in the repo, so the precondition (the header is not stripped upstream) is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed at views.py:26 (acl.py:8-10) correctly aborts 403 when the grant is missing, but it keys on the unauthenticated header string; no signature or session check exists in the repo, and no proxy config is present.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 trusts the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header and acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, so spoofing is possible if the header isn't stripped and set by an upstream proxy, but the repo (only views.py and acl.py) can't show whether such a proxy exists.
